title: Reading Literature at B1 and Beyond: How to Analyse a Text
paragraphs: Literary analysis is sometimes presented as a mysterious art practised only by academics in quiet libraries. In reality, it is a set of learnable skills — a toolkit for asking better questions of a text and finding richer answers. When you read a novel, a poem, or a short story and ask not just "what happened?" but "why is this written this way?" and "what does this mean?", you have begun to analyse. This is not a specialist pursuit — it is what engaged readers do naturally when they encounter texts that matter to them.

The first and most fundamental tool of literary analysis is attention to language. Writers make choices about every word, every sentence, every image. These choices are not accidental — or, when they are accidental, that is itself interesting. When Emily Brontë describes the moors in Wuthering Heights as wild and bleak, she is not simply providing geographical information; she is establishing an emotional and symbolic atmosphere that mirrors her characters' inner states. When Gabriel García Márquez opens One Hundred Years of Solitude with "Many years later, as he faced the firing squad, Colonel Aureliano Buendía was to remember that distant afternoon when his father took him to discover ice," he is using time in a way that immediately signals the kind of story this will be.

The second tool is attention to structure. How is the text organised? Does it move chronologically or does it play with time? Is it told from a single perspective or multiple ones? Does it begin with a striking image and return to it at the end? Structural choices shape meaning as powerfully as individual words. A novel told in reverse chronological order says something different from the same events told forwards, even if every sentence is identical. Structure is not packaging — it is meaning.

The third tool is awareness of context — historical, cultural, and biographical. A text is produced by a particular person, in a particular place and time, for a particular audience, under particular constraints. Reading Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four without knowing something about Stalinist totalitarianism reduces it to science fiction; knowing its context reveals it as a sharp political satire with real stakes. Context does not determine meaning — the same text can be read differently across different times and places — but it enriches our understanding enormously.

The fourth tool is intertextuality — awareness of the relationships between texts. Great works of literature do not exist in isolation; they are in conversation with earlier texts, responding to, challenging, or subverting them. Milton's Paradise Lost rewrites Genesis. Salman Rushdie's Midnight's Children is in explicit conversation with Laurence Sterne's Tristram Shandy. Knowing these connections deepens reading. But even without specialist knowledge, a reader who notices that a text feels like a fairy tale, or like a newspaper report, or like a prayer, is already thinking intertextually.

The fifth and perhaps most important tool is willingness to sit with uncertainty. Great literature does not always yield its meaning easily, and a text that yields its meaning too easily is often not very interesting. A poem that you can summarise in one sentence is probably not doing the work of a poem. Ambiguity — the productive uncertainty about what something means — is not a failure of the text; it is, very often, its highest achievement. The willingness to stay with a difficult text, to read it again, to change your interpretation, to hold multiple meanings simultaneously, is what separates engaged from passive reading.

None of these tools requires advanced academic knowledge to use. They require curiosity, patience, and the willingness to ask questions that may not have final answers. They require treating the text as a partner in a conversation, not a puzzle to be solved. And they reward that treatment generously — great literature, read with attention and care, offers gifts that no other art form quite matches.

vocab.definition: the relationship between texts; the way in which one text refers to, uses, or transforms another
vocab.example: "Intertextuality — recognising that texts are in conversation with earlier ones — deepens reading."

vocab.definition: the quality of having more than one possible meaning; productive uncertainty
vocab.example: "Ambiguity is not a failure — it is often a text's highest achievement."

vocab.definition: the use of irony, exaggeration, or ridicule to expose and criticise folly or vice
vocab.example: "Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four is a sharp political satire with real historical stakes."
